ai_summary: Great Britain's wind fleet is currently generating 8.1 GW, with Scottish wind output estimated at 1.8 GW, representing 17.8% of installed Scottish wind capacity. Scotland's electricity system continues to deliver exceptional clean performance with a carbon intensity of 0 gCO2/kWh, standing in stark contrast to the GB-wide average of 178 gCO2/kWh. However, structural cross-border transmission limits mean zero-carbon power cannot fully flow southward. As a result, 578 MWh of Scottish generation has been curtailed so far today through Balancing Mechanism bids, incurring a constraint cost of about £38,660. To replace this lost clean volume, fossil-fuel thermal plants were dispatched elsewhere on the grid, consuming an estimated 109,820 m3 of gas and emitting an additional 202 tonnes CO2 into the atmosphere. Annualizing today's constraint expenditure yields an estimated total yearly curtailment cost of £14 million. When socialized across standard British electricity consumption, this adds an estimated increase of roughly £0.05/MWh to consumer invoices across the UK. This persistent transmission friction highlights how grid bottlenecks simultaneously elevate system costs for billpayers and force unnecessary carbon emissions onto the broader national network.
